stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Standard models predict that raising a wage floor reduces employment, since some jobs stop being worth their cost to employers. Studying one statewide increase, economist Lena Ostrowski compared towns where a single firm hires most local workers with towns where many firms compete for staff. Employment dipped slightly in the competitive towns but rose in the single-firm towns, and nearly all the added workers there were longtime residents who had not been seeking work, not newcomers. Ostrowski hypothesizes that before the increase, ______
choices: the dominant firms had offered too few openings to employ every resident who wanted a job
firms in both kinds of towns had paid workers less than their labor was worth to the firm
the dominant firms had kept pay low enough that many residents judged a job not worth taking
residents of the competitive towns had been willing to relocate to wherever pay was rising
explanation: The puzzle is that a higher wage floor raised employment, but only in single-firm towns, and the new workers were local residents who had not been looking for work. One explanation fits all three details. Where one firm dominates, it can set pay low because workers have nowhere else to go, and at that low pay some residents decide a job isn't worth taking. When the floor forces pay up, those residents start working. In competitive towns, competition had already pushed pay up, so the floor only raised costs, and employment dipped as the standard model predicts.

A.why: You saw that the new workers were people who hadn't been working, but you blamed a shortage of jobs instead of a shortage of willing workers. If the firms had too few openings, making each worker more expensive would lead them to cut jobs, not add them. This choice predicts employment falling in single-firm towns, which is the opposite of what the passage reports.

B.why: You spotted the underpayment explanation but applied it to every town. If firms in competitive towns had also been underpaying, the floor should have raised employment there too. Instead it dipped, so this choice ignores the comparison group, which is the key detail.

D.why: Migration would explain a rise in one place and a dip in another, but the passage says the added workers were longtime residents, not newcomers. This choice explains the pattern by assuming something the passage rules out.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Most algae-eating reef fish feed in sunlit shallows, where algae grow fastest. Divers were therefore surprised to find juveniles of one such goby clustered on deep, dim ledges where algae are sparse, while adults stayed in the shallows. Juveniles on the ledges grew more slowly than juveniles kept in shallow pens that excluded predators, yet they outlived unprotected juveniles released on shallow reefs from which all adults had been removed. The team hypothesizes that ______
choices: adult gobies defend the shallow feeding areas and force the juveniles down to the ledges
for juveniles, the safety of the ledges outweighs the faster growth the shallows would allow
for juveniles, the faster growth the shallows allow outweighs the danger of feeding there
predators in the shallows will kill any juvenile goby that does not shelter on the ledges
explanation: The surprise is that juveniles live where food is poor. The two comparisons give both sides of a trade-off. Juveniles in the shallows grow faster when protected from predators, so the shallows offer better food. Unprotected juveniles in the shallows die sooner than juveniles on the ledges, even with no adults around, so the shallows are more dangerous. Juveniles choose the ledges anyway, so the hypothesis has to be that, for them, safety matters more than faster growth.

A.why: Competition with adults sounds scientific, but you ignored a key detail of the setup. The unprotected juveniles were released on reefs where all the adults had been removed, and they still did worse than juveniles on the ledges. Adults can't be what drives the pattern.

C.why: You identified the trade-off correctly but settled it in the wrong direction. If faster growth outweighed the danger, juveniles would gather in the shallows. The passage says they gather on the ledges, so this choice describes the opposite of what the gobies actually do.

D.why: You saw that predation drives the pattern, then made the claim stronger than the evidence allows. The passage says ledge juveniles outlived unprotected ones. It doesn't say every unsheltered juvenile dies. 'Any' and 'will' go beyond that evidence.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Because circulating memory T cells travel throughout the body, immunologists long assumed that how quickly a person clears a repeat skin infection depends mainly on these cells. Kenji Arata tested this in volunteers who had recovered from a mild infection on one forearm. Biopsies showed equal numbers of circulating memory T cells in both forearms, yet when re-exposed, the previously infected forearm cleared the pathogen within hours while the other forearm took several days. Arata hypothesizes that ______
choices: circulating memory T cells contribute nothing to clearing a repeat infection of the skin.
some other immune cells remain in skin that was once infected and speed clearance there.
the number of circulating memory T cells in a forearm determines how fast it clears the pathogen.
repeat infections are cleared faster in the skin than in any other tissue of the body.
explanation: The surprise is that the two forearms had the same number of circulating memory T cells but cleared the pathogen at very different speeds. So the circulating cells can't explain the gap. The only thing that sets the fast forearm apart is that it was infected before. A hypothesis that something stays behind in once-infected skin and speeds clearance there explains every detail, and it claims no more than the passage supports.

A.why: You correctly saw that circulating cells don't explain the difference, then pushed that to 'nothing.' The other forearm still cleared the pathogen in several days, and circulating cells may have done that work. The passage only shows that they don't account for the gap, not that they do nothing.

C.why: You finished with the older assumption that the passage sets up to undercut. Both forearms had equal numbers of circulating memory T cells but cleared the pathogen at different speeds, so that number can't be what decides the speed.

D.why: The study compares two patches of skin, not skin with other tissues. You picked a claim that sounds scientific but rests on a comparison the passage never makes.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: At Kessa Point, a coastal settlement occupied for about six centuries, fish bones are abundant in the earliest layers but nearly absent from the later ones. The change is puzzling: heavily worn bone fishhooks are just as common in the later layers, and shells from the same period show that nearby waters stayed rich in the same fish species. Meanwhile, an inland village 30 kilometers away, which has no fishhooks at all, holds large quantities of those species' bones dating only to Kessa Point's later centuries. The researchers hypothesize that ______
choices: Kessa Point's later residents kept fishing but sent much of their catch to the inland village.
the inland village supplied Kessa Point with fish after Kessa Point's own waters were overfished.
Kessa Point's later residents ate fish only after cleaning them at camps away from the settlement.
Kessa Point's later residents traded away their fishhooks and stopped catching fish themselves.
explanation: Hold all four details at once. The worn hooks mean Kessa Point kept fishing. The rich waters mean the fish were still there. The bones are missing from Kessa Point. The same species turn up, in the same centuries, at a village that couldn't catch them because it had no hooks. The one explanation that fits all of this is that Kessa Point caught the fish and they ended up inland.

B.why: You saw that the two sites were connected but reversed the direction. The inland village had no hooks, and the shells show Kessa Point's waters were not exhausted.

C.why: This explains why the bones are missing from Kessa Point but ignores the inland village, which is exactly where those bones appear. The cleaning camps are never mentioned, so you added an assumption to explain part of the puzzle while leaving the key clue unused.

D.why: Heavily worn hooks are just as common in Kessa Point's later layers, so its residents were still using them to fish. They did not give up fishing.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Permeable pavement reduces stormwater runoff by letting rain pass through its pores into a gravel base and then into the soil below. Over time, fine sediment clogs the pores, and engineers have generally blamed declining performance on this clogging. In a five-year trial, however, sections built over clay soil and sections built over sandy soil lost surface infiltration at the same rate, yet by the end the clay sections were reducing runoff far less than the sandy ones. The engineers hypothesize that ______
choices: the pavement's pores clog more quickly over clay soil than they do over sandy soil.
clogging of the pores has no effect on how much runoff permeable pavement prevents.
clearing sediment from the clay sections' pores would bring them up to the sandy sections' level.
the clay sections fall short because water drains slowly from their gravel base into the soil.
explanation: Surface clogging was the same for both soils, so it can't explain why the clay sections did worse. The only difference left is what lies beneath the base: clay or sand. If water can't drain quickly out of the gravel into clay, the base fills up and stops absorbing runoff. That explains the gap without contradicting the matched infiltration rates.

A.why: The passage says both soil types lost surface infiltration at the same rate. Faster clogging over clay is ruled out directly.

B.why: You saw that clogging doesn't explain the difference, then concluded that it does nothing at all. Both kinds of sections did clog, and that may well have hurt both. The trial only shows that clogging doesn't account for the gap between them.

C.why: You fell back on the popular view that the passage undercuts. Both sections clogged equally, so clearing the pores would leave the clay sections' drainage problem, and the gap, where it was.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: In many regions, small earthquakes become more frequent when groundwater rises, because water seeping into faults weakens the friction holding them in place. In the Varra Basin, however, small quakes peak each year in late summer, when groundwater is at its lowest. Unlike the faults in those other regions, the Varra Basin's faults lie directly beneath a thick aquifer, whose water adds weight that presses the two sides of each fault together. The researchers hypothesize that ______
choices: water seeping into the Varra Basin's faults in late summer weakens the friction along them.
the aquifer's weight, when it is greatest, pushes the Varra Basin's faults past their limit.
the aquifer, lighter in late summer, presses less firmly on the faults and lets them slip.
faults dry out as groundwater falls, growing more brittle and more likely to fracture.
explanation: Here the usual effect is flipped: quakes peak when groundwater is lowest. The detail that sets the Varra Basin apart is that the aquifer's weight clamps its faults together. When the water drains in late summer, that clamping weakens, so the faults slip more easily. This uses only the mechanism the passage gives you, and it points in the right direction.

A.why: You applied the original effect from other regions. In late summer the Varra Basin's groundwater is at its lowest, so there is the least water seeping into its faults, not the most.

B.why: You correctly saw that weight matters but got the direction backward. The aquifer is heaviest when groundwater is high, yet quakes peak when it is low. More clamping weight resists slipping.

D.why: This sounds scientific, but nothing in the passage says dry faults become brittle. It skips the one mechanism the passage does give you, the aquifer's weight pressing on the faults.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Copper etching plates wear with each printing, so fine lines grow fainter in later impressions; if a plate cracks, the crack appears in every impression printed afterward. Two surviving impressions of Ilse Varn's 1652 etching Harbor at Dusk share an identical stray scratch in one corner. One has faint fine lines and no crack. The other shows a crack across the sky, yet its fine lines are crisp, and under magnification they follow slightly different paths from the faint ones. Curator Tomas Bell hypothesizes that ______
choices: the cracked impression was pulled after the plate's worn lines had been cut into it again.
the cracked impression was pulled first, before repeated printing wore down the fine lines.
the two impressions were pulled from separate plates that Varn etched at different times.
the uncracked impression's faint lines came from light inking rather than from a worn plate.
explanation: The identical scratch shows that both impressions came from one plate. A crack shows up in every later impression, so the uncracked impression must have been printed before the crack, and the cracked one after. That means the later impression has the crisper lines. Lines that follow slightly different paths explain how: the worn lines were cut into the plate again before the cracked impression was printed.

B.why: You read crisp lines as a sign of an early impression, which is the obvious first step, and stopped there. If the cracked impression had come first, the crack would also appear in the later, faint one, and it doesn't.

C.why: Two plates would explain the differing line paths, but both impressions share an identical stray scratch. That marks them as coming from the same plate.

D.why: The passage never mentions inking. Light inking wouldn't explain why the lines follow different paths, and it wouldn't explain the order the crack reveals.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: In single-meal tests, adding vitamin C to a plant-based meal sharply increases how much iron the body absorbs from that meal. Yet in an eight-week trial, participants who took vitamin C with every meal showed little overall change in their iron stores compared with participants who did not. The exception was a small group who began the trial iron-deficient: they gained iron substantially. The researchers hypothesize that ______
choices: vitamin C does not raise iron absorption at all outside of single-meal laboratory tests.
iron-deficient people can absorb iron from plant foods only when vitamin C is present.
eight weeks is too short a period for vitamin C's effect on iron stores to appear.
the body cuts its iron absorption once stores are adequate, offsetting vitamin C's boost.
explanation: Two results have to fit together. Over eight weeks, vitamin C did almost nothing for most people but did help those who started out deficient. What separates the groups is how much iron they already had. If the body limits absorption once its stores are adequate, the boost would fade for people with enough iron and last for people who were short.

A.why: You took the overall null result and made it absolute. The iron-deficient group gained substantially during the trial, so vitamin C clearly did something outside single-meal tests.

B.why: The word 'only' is strength creep. The trial shows that deficient people gained iron with vitamin C, not that they can't absorb plant iron without it.

C.why: You ignored the comparison group. The iron-deficient participants did gain iron within the same eight weeks, so the trial was long enough for an effect to appear.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Hand-hygiene compliance at Linden Hospital rose from 60 percent to 90 percent after gel dispensers were installed beside every bed, according to audits in which trained observers stood on the ward. Yet the rate of infections patients acquired in the hospital did not change. Counters hidden inside the dispensers, which staff did not know about, logged heavy use during audit hours but only modest use at all other times. Hospital officials hypothesize that ______
choices: the gel was too weak to kill the bacteria responsible for most of the hospital's infections.
the observers miscounted how often staff cleaned their hands while the audits were underway.
staff cleaned their hands far more often while being watched than at other times of day.
cleaning hands more often does little to reduce the infections patients acquire in hospitals.
explanation: The hidden counters are the key. Staff didn't know about them, and they show heavy use only while observers were present. So the audits captured behavior under observation, and the rest of the day looked very different. With everyday hand cleaning only modestly better, it makes sense that infection rates didn't move.

A.why: This sounds like a scientific explanation, but the passage says nothing about how strong the gel is. It also leaves out the hidden counters, the one detail that explains the puzzle.

B.why: You saw that the audits were misleading but blamed the counting. The hidden counters confirm heavy use during audit hours, so the observers recorded what they saw correctly. The problem is that what they saw was not typical.

D.why: This assumes hand cleaning really did increase across the day, but the counters show only modest use outside audits. It also stretches one hospital's result into a general claim about all hospitals.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Removing trees from a watershed usually increases streamflow, since fewer trees are drawing water from the soil and releasing it through their needles or leaves. Yet after bark beetles killed most of the pines in the Ossa Valley, leaving them standing but bare, annual streamflow fell. With the needles gone, far more sunlight reached the snowpack beneath the trees, and the snow there vanished weeks earlier than before, yet spring soil moisture did not rise. Hydrologists hypothesize that ______
choices: the dead pines kept drawing water from the soil even after their needles had fallen.
more of the snowpack passed into the air as vapor, outweighing the water the trees no longer used.
the snow melted earlier and reached the stream before the season when flow was measured.
removing trees from a watershed reduces streamflow in most forested valleys.
explanation: Follow the snow. It vanished weeks earlier once sunlight reached it. Soil moisture didn't rise, so the snow didn't soak into the ground, and streamflow fell, so it didn't reach the stream either. The remaining path is straight into the air. If enough snow was lost that way, it would cancel out the water the dead trees stopped using, and annual flow would drop.

A.why: Nothing in the passage suggests that dead, bare trees keep drawing water. You reached for an explanation that sounds plausible but uses none of the details about sunlight and snow.

C.why: You noticed that the snow disappeared earlier and assumed it melted into the stream. The passage measures annual streamflow, which would include early meltwater, and that flow fell.

D.why: One valley's reversal doesn't overturn the usual pattern the passage describes, and the word 'most' is strength creep. The hypothesis has to explain the Ossa Valley, not rewrite the general rule.
